body:
Regarding BEM, [this article](http://csswizardry.com/2015/03/more-transparent-ui-code-with-namespaces/) was an eye opener for me.

This goes a step further than BEM but more importantly explains why BEM is designed this way and suggest a naming convention for common components, modifier classes, layout classes and so on.

In a nutshell, they suggest adding a one-letter prefix to our BEM classes, to explain what this kind of class this is. The more important prefixes are:

* `c-` for a component, like a piece of UI. Modifications in those classes should not leak to other components.
* `o-` for a (meta) object which is more an abstraction of a concept, shared accross several components. Change in those classes will have important impact in different parts. Dangerous.
* `u-` for utility classes. Theses can be easily added to the HTML markup to slightly change a display, and can be used in any components. This include classes like `u-disabled` or `u-clearfix` for example.
* `t-` is for theming. Those are purely cosmetic changes. Ideally, you can remove all `t-` classes and still have a usable component. Changing the `t-` classes will result in a new look'n'feel but to do alter behavior.
* `is-` and `has-` are here to signify a state of a current piece of ui. Something like `has-results`, `is-loading`.
* `_` is for hacks. Anything prefixed with this is to avoid a brower bug, or do something ugly. We might do this kind of hack, but better mark them as such.
* `js-` is for marking DOM-element for JavaScript. It is not used in any CSS file, it is just here to provide an easy selector for JS bindings.

I'm not saying we should use those prefixes as-is, but those are important separation we need to keep in mind to:

* Share common classes accross several widgets
* Use specific styling for specific widgets that do not leak into the global css namespace and collide with user-defined styles
* Separate styling (css) from behavior (js)
* Allow users to customise the appearance without breaking the behavior
